watch_sentences: A donor-advised fund is a charitable account held at a public charity, called the sponsoring organization.
Advisors choose the investment options within the sponsor's investment policy.
Altruist shows you every detail the current sponsor's grant form will ask for, in one click.
Because DAF assets belong to the sponsor, a transfer works like a grant: open a DAF in Altruist, then ask the current sponsor to grant the balance to the new fund.
Because the sponsor already owns the assets, they sit outside the client's taxable estate.
DAFs on Altruist are sponsored by Endaoment, a 501(c)(3) public charity that is the legal owner of DAF assets.
Endaoment, a public charity.
Grant and investment recommendations are advisory only and subject to Endaoment's approval.
How fast it completes is up to the current sponsor.
Once the assets go to the sponsor, the client cannot get them back or redirect them to anything other than charity.
Some sponsors accept illiquid assets, like real estate, stakes in private businesses, cryptocurrency, and art.
Sponsoring organizations may set their own inactivity policies.
The public charity that sponsors DAFs owns the assets, confirms the receiving organization is eligible, approves and disburses each grant, and handles IRS reporting.
The sponsor approves all grant recommendations.
The sponsor has the final say
The sponsor issues the contribution receipt and annual acknowledgment, delivered through Altruist's Document Center.
The sponsor legally owns the assets, and its policy sets what's eligible.
These gifts have to be appraised and pass the sponsor's due diligence first, so they take longer than cash or stock, and the sponsor can decline.
Who sponsors Altruist DAFs?
Your client contributes cash or stock to the DAF sponsor, who administers the account.
